# What happens when mpc_alpha is too large or too small?

> **Current answer:** In this simulation, an excessive mpc_alpha penalizes contact force, leading to insufficient support force; reducing it increases the foot bottom force. The authors set the target of approximately half of the robot's weight being supported by the trot foot. Comments warn that an overly small weight may make the real machine sensitive to acceleration changes and cause severe oscillation, so it cannot be solely focused on increasing contact force.

## Key terms

- Whole-Body Control (WBC) (全身控制)
- Quadratic Programming (QP) (二次规划)
- Model Predictive Control (MPC) (模型预测控制)
- Joint Torque (关节力矩)
- Latency Jitter (时延抖动)
- Dynamics (动力学)

## Problem and symptoms

- MPC contact force penalty weight is too large, leading to insufficient support force; WBC floating base weight is too large, leading to contact force instability.
- Foot bottom force is small when mpc_alpha=0.1.
- Foot bottom force has sparse large peaks and causes fall when floating_base_weight=1e14.

## Environment

- Four-legged robot trot gait simulation; robot mass example is approximately 20 kg, total gravity approximately 200 N.

## Priority diagnostics

- Compare foot bottom force, body angular velocity, and linear velocity curves under different weights.

## Possible causes

- mpc_alpha is a force amplitude penalty term; too large suppresses contact force; too small may amplify sensitivity to acceleration changes in real machines.
- Overly large floating_base_weight over-pressures the relaxation cost between dynamics and contact force balance.

## Attempts

- Test mpc_alpha=0.1, 0.0002, and ~5e-5; test floating_base_weight=1e-6, 1e6, and 1e14.

## Effective fixes

- Reduce mpc_alpha to a level that can generate nearly single-foot half-body weight contact force during trot support phase, and moderately increase floating_base_weight.

## Result

- Foot bottom force peak increases from 80 N to 110 N when floating_base_weight increases from 1e-6 to 1e6, and speed fluctuation becomes smaller; at 1e14, it becomes unstable and falls.

## Limitations

- Numerical values derived from a specific four-legged simulation; the author explicitly states the conclusion is still to be verified by others; cannot directly be applied to humanoid robots or different normalization cost definitions.

## Safety notes

- Weight scanning must set contact force, moment, and state limits; 1e14 scale has already caused instability in simulation, cannot be directly applied to real machines.

## Image and visual evidence

- Image 'mpc_alpha=0.1' simultaneously shows four-legged simulation and foot bottom force curve; curve amplitude is low, consistent with the text's description of insufficient support force, but the screenshot itself does not provide a unified coordinate calibration.
- Image 'floating_base_weight=1e6' shows a regular periodic foot bottom force waveform with peak around 110 N; can be compared with the text's description of ~80 N at 1e-6.
- Image 'floating_base_weight=1e14' shows sparse and large foot bottom force peaks, corresponding to the text's description of unstable contact force and fall.

## Applicability boundary

- Only applicable to MPC with similar cost definition, mass normalization, and force scaling; specific values need to be re-identified.
